list_one.title: A 32-bit length taken from the wire sizes a byte array before any payload arrives (ValueReader.readBytes)
list_one.impact: A peer that speaks to this decoder can make the client JVM commit up to ~2 GiB of heap per value, at a cost of five bytes per attempt and with no payload to send. The result is OutOfMemoryError in the process hosting the client library, which is the consuming application, not merely the broker connection — a Java OOM is not contained to the thread that triggered it, and repeated attempts hold the allocation attempt for as long as the collector fights for the space. Availability of the whole client application is the asset at risk. The same shape appears inside a field table, where the enclosing TruncatedInputStream cannot help: a table whose declared length is six bytes can still carry `x` plus a declared length of 2147483646, and the array is allocated before the truncated stream refuses the read.

list_one.title: An untrusted 64-bit timestamp is multiplied by 1000 with no overflow check
list_one.impact: The peer obtains Date values outside the range the seconds encoding is supposed to be able to express, including a far-past date from a far-future input. Consuming code that treats a message timestamp as age, freshness or expiry receives a value that does not round-trip. The attacker gains almost nothing they did not already have — an AMQP timestamp is peer-supplied by design, so any in-range value was already theirs to choose — which is why this is recorded as informational rather than as a risk.
list_one.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. The eight bytes come from the stream and the product is computed in `long` arithmetic, which wraps silently in Java. Any seconds value above 9223372036854775 (or below its negative) produces a millisecond value with the opposite sign or an unrelated magnitude. Reached from the public readTimestamp() at lines 274-278 and from readFieldValue case 'T' at line 178. This is the third neighbour WEB-26 names in the same family — a value multiplied without an overflow check — and it sits in the same file as F-001 and F-002.

list_one.title: Mutual recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray carries no depth counter
list_one.impact: A few tens of kilobytes of nested field arrays exhausts the JVM stack and raises StackOverflowError. That is an Error, not the IOException the surrounding code is written to handle: nothing in this class catches it, so it unwinds past the decode loop and kills the thread that reads the connection rather than closing the connection cleanly. The consuming application is left with a dead reader thread, which is a harder failure to detect and recover from than a protocol error. Depth also multiplies the memory cost of F-001, since each level can declare its own oversized value.
list_one.evidence:
The cycle closes twice, both times on data the peer chooses:

  readFieldValue (line 158) -- case 'F' (line 180) --> readTable (line 139) --> readFieldValue (line 150)
  readFieldValue (line 158) -- case 'A' (line 183) --> readArray (line 237) --> readFieldValue (line 245)

The three signatures are `static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)` (158), `private static Map<String, Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)` (139) and `private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)` (237). None carries a depth parameter, and no counter is kept anywhere in the class — WEB-26's test is exactly this: walk the recursive entry points and look for a depth argument in the signature. Each additional level of nesting costs the peer five bytes inside a field array (the type octet 'A' plus a four-byte length) or six inside a table (a zero-length short string name, the octet 'F', a four-byte length). The recursion is driven by `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` (line 244) and `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` (line 148), neither of which bounds nesting.

list_one.title: The build generates and ships protocol classes from a working copy the manifest neither pins nor verifies
list_one.impact: The generated AMQP protocol classes are compiled into the published jar, so whoever controls the contents of the codegen working copy on the build machine chooses source code that ships to every consumer, without that change appearing in this repository's diff. This is the shape of a build-path compromise rather than a demonstrated one: reaching it requires write access to the build host or to whatever clones that directory, so no attacker outside the build environment is claimed here.
list_one.evidence: pom.xml:102-112 declares `deps.dir` = `${basedir}/deps` and `codegen.dir` = `${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen`, documented in the same comment as "a directory containing a working copy of rabbitmq-codegen and rabbitmq-server". pom.xml:597-637 binds groovy-maven-plugin to `generate-sources` to run `generate_amqp_sources.groovy`, described in its own comment as "a proxy to execute a Python script" — `${basedir}/codegen.py` — against `${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json`, writing AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java into `${project.build.directory}/generated-sources`. pom.xml:640-658 then adds that directory to the main compile through build-helper-maven-plugin `add-source`. The plugin runs Groovy 2.4.21, injected as a plugin dependency at pom.xml:81 and 665-668. What the manifest pins is `codegen.spec_version` 0.9.1, which selects a file name; it declares no revision, checksum or signature for the working copy that file comes from, and the step that obtains that working copy is not in the manifest at all.

list_two.title: The timestamp decoder multiplies an attacker-chosen 64-bit value by 1000 with no overflow check
list_two.impact: An application that reads the AMQP timestamp property for ordering, expiry, deduplication or audit receives a Date the peer selected freely, including one far in the past or the future, from an encoded seconds value that looks unremarkable. Nothing is corrupted inside the library; the damage, if any, is in the consumer's use of the value. A peer that can set the timestamp field at all already influences it, so the extra capability is the ability to reach millisecond values that a non-wrapping conversion could not produce, and to do so without the encoded seconds looking anomalous to anything that inspects the frame.

list_two.title: The default build executes generator scripts over an external specification checkout that the manifest does not pin, and compiles the result into the published jar
list_two.impact: Whoever controls the contents of `deps/rabbitmq_codegen` on the machine that performs a release controls Java source that is compiled into the published library, with no signature or hash standing in the way. This is the shape SUP-04 exists for: the malicious content never has to appear in this repository's source tree, only in the build input, and the released jar carries it to every consumer. The same execution also runs a Groovy script and a Python script under the build's identity at generate-sources, so a compromise of either script file is code execution in the release environment.
list_two.evidence: The plugin is bound to the default lifecycle, not to a profile (pom.xml lines 595-638): goal `execute` at phase `generate-sources`, `<source>${groovy-scripts.dir}/generate_amqp_sources.groovy</source>`, with `<script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script>` and `<spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json</spec>`. The properties block resolves `${codegen.dir}` to `${basedir}/deps/rabbitmq_codegen` and documents it as "a working copy of rabbitmq-codegen"; `${codegen.spec_version}` is `0.9.1`, which pins the file name of the specification, not its content. build-helper-maven-plugin then adds `${project.build.directory}/generated-sources/src/main/java` to the compile roots (lines 640-658), so whatever those scripts emit is compiled into the artifact that maven-jar-plugin packages and central-publishing-maven-plugin publishes. Nowhere in the manifest is there a digest, a checksum verification, a signature check or a pinned revision for the contents of `${deps.dir}` — grep for `http://` returns only XML namespace declarations, so the risk here is not an unverified download inside the pom but an unverified working copy the pom consumes.

list_two.title: The peer chooses whether the decoder fails with a protocol exception or with an unchecked one, on a path declared to throw IOException
list_two.impact: A caller that closes the connection cleanly on IOException — the contract this method declares, and the one MalformedFrameException was written for — does not catch this. The peer can therefore steer the failure onto whatever generic handler sits above, which is at best a different shutdown path than the protocol-error one and at worst none, leaving the connection thread to die without the orderly close and listener notification the IOException path provides. The attacker gains a choice of failure mode on a client they were already able to disconnect, which is a small gain, not a new capability.

list_two.title: Mutual recursion between the field-value, table and array decoders carries no depth counter
list_two.impact: A peer that sends a deeply nested field table or field array drives the decoding thread into a StackOverflowError at a cost of a few bytes per stack frame. StackOverflowError is an Error, not an IOException, so it does not travel the path that MalformedFrameException (line 217) was written for: a caller that closes the connection cleanly on IOException will not catch it. The reachable outcome is the death of the connection's I/O thread, plus the per-level stream and map objects allocated on the way down. This is the neighbouring class WEB-26 names alongside the allocation in F-001, and both are reachable through the same readFieldValue switch.
list_two.evidence:
The cycle is closed inside this one file and no signature on it carries a depth parameter:
  line 158  static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)
  line 181      case 'F':  value = readTable(in);   // -> line 139 readTable
  line 184      case 'A':  value = readArray(in);   // -> line 237 readArray
  line 150      readTable:  Object value = readFieldValue(tableIn);
  line 245      readArray:  Object value = readFieldValue(arrayIn);
readTable is declared `private static Map<String,Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)` (line 139) and readArray `private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)` (line 237): neither takes a level argument, and no counter, ThreadLocal or configured maximum appears anywhere in the file. Each level of nesting costs the peer a handful of bytes — inside an array, one type byte 'A' plus a four-byte length is five bytes per frame of stack — while each level allocates a fresh TruncatedInputStream, a fresh DataInputStream and, for a table, a HashMap (lines 145-147, 241-243).

list_two.title: A 32-bit length taken off the socket sizes a byte array before any payload arrives, behind a cast guard that is not a limit
list_two.impact: A peer that can write to the socket — a hostile or compromised broker, or an on-path attacker on a connection without TLS — commits up to roughly 2 GB of client heap per decoded value by sending four bytes. The result is an OutOfMemoryError in the process that embeds this library, which is an availability failure of the consuming application rather than of the broker. Because the byte-vector and long-string types are legal inside a field table, the same trick can be repeated per table entry within one frame, so the peer does not need many round trips.
